q: Which compound gives the IR spectrum shown? (There is no significant absorption above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> or between 1600 and 1800 cm<sup>−1</sup>.)
h: A medium, sharp band in the triple-bond region (2100–2260 cm<sup>−1</sup>) with no band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> narrows it down quickly.
w: The only band beyond the C–H stretches is a medium, sharp absorption at 2250 cm−1, the C≡N stretch of a nitrile. The polar C≡N bond gives a stronger band than a C≡C stretch. The answer is butanenitrile. Nothing above 3000 cm−1 rules out O–H, N–H and ≡C–H, and nothing at 1700 cm−1 rules out C=O.
x: A terminal alkyne shows a strong, sharp ≡C–H stretch near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a weak C≡C stretch near 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup>; neither is in this spectrum.
Butanal would show a strong C=O band near 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup> and the aldehyde C–H pair near 2720 and 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Butylamine (a primary amine) would show two N–H stretches between 3300 and 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup> and has no triple bond to absorb at 2250 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Which compound gives the IR spectrum shown?
h: Look at the two regions that decide most problems: 3200–3600 cm<sup>−1</sup> and 1650–1800 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
w: A strong, broad band centered near 3340 cm−1 is a hydrogen-bonded alcohol O–H, and the strong band near 1070 cm−1 is the C–O stretch. There is no C=O band, and all C–H stretches are below 3000 cm−1 (sp3 only). The answer is cyclohexanol.
x: Cyclohexanone has a strong C=O stretch near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no O–H band.
Cyclohexene shows a vinylic =C–H stretch just above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C=C stretch near 1650 cm<sup>−1</sup>, but no broad O–H band.
A carboxylic acid shows an O–H band so broad it spans about 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>, plus a strong C=O near 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup>; there is no C=O band here.

q: The IR spectrum shown has an extremely broad O–H absorption that spans about 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> (it overlaps the C–H stretches) and a strong band at 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which compound is it?
h: Several choices have an O–H or a C=O. What makes an O–H band reach all the way down to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>?
w: Carboxylic acids exist as strongly hydrogen-bonded dimers, so the O–H stretch is spread over roughly 2500–3300 cm−1 and buries the C–H bands. Together with the C=O stretch at 1710 cm−1 (typical of a dimeric acid), this identifies butanoic acid.
x: 4-Hydroxy-2-butanone has both an alcohol O–H and a ketone C=O, but an alcohol O–H band is centered near 3400 cm<sup>−1</sup> and does not extend down to 2500 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Methyl propanoate is an ester: strong C=O near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> and strong C–O bands near 1200 cm<sup>−1</sup>, but no O–H at all.
1,4-Butanediol has a broad alcohol O–H near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> but no C=O, so it cannot explain the strong 1710 cm<sup>−1</sup> band.

q: An amine-containing compound gives the IR spectrum shown. The only band between 1500 and 1800 cm<sup>−1</sup> is a medium band at 1600 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which compound is it?
h: Count the N–H stretching bands, then ask whether a C=O band is present.
w: Two medium N–H bands (3370 and 3290 cm−1, the asymmetric and symmetric stretches of an NH2 group) mean a primary amine or a primary amide. The medium 1600 cm−1 band is the N–H bend; there is no strong C=O band. The answer is butylamine (1-butanamine).
x: Diethylamine is a secondary amine with one N–H, so it shows only a single weak N–H band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Triethylamine is a tertiary amine with no N–H bond, so there is no absorption above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Butanamide also shows two N–H bands, but its amide C=O gives a strong band near 1650–1690 cm<sup>−1</sup>, which is missing here.

q: Rank the C=O stretching wavenumbers of compounds I–IV from highest to lowest.
h: Electron-withdrawing groups on the carbonyl carbon stiffen the C=O bond; lone-pair donation into the C=O gives it single-bond character.
w: A higher C=O wavenumber means more double-bond character (larger force constant). Chlorine withdraws inductively and donates poorly, so the acid chloride absorbs highest (~1800 cm−1). In the ester the inductive pull of the extra oxygen outweighs its resonance donation (~1740 cm−1). A ketone is the reference (~1715 cm−1). Nitrogen donates its lone pair strongly, so the amide C=O is lowest (~1650–1690 cm−1). The order is I > II > III > IV.
x: This reverses the trend: resonance donation from N lowers, not raises, the C=O bond order, so the amide is lowest.
The acid chloride is above the ester; chlorine withdraws electrons and is a much poorer π donor than the ester oxygen.
Esters absorb above ketones (about 1740 vs 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>) because the ester oxygen's inductive withdrawal dominates its resonance donation.

q: Which compound has the lowest C=O stretching wavenumber?
h: Two effects matter: conjugation with a C=C and ring strain in small rings. Which way does each move the C=O band?
w: Conjugation with a C=C lets the C=O π electrons delocalize, lowering the C=O bond order and its stretching wavenumber by about 30–40 cm−1. 2-Cyclohexen-1-one absorbs near 1680 cm−1. Ring strain does the opposite: the smaller the ring, the higher the C=O band.
x: Cyclohexanone is the unstrained, unconjugated reference, absorbing near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>, higher than the conjugated enone.
Cyclopentanone's ring strain raises the C=O stretch to about 1745 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Cyclobutanone is even more strained and absorbs near 1780 cm<sup>−1</sup>, the highest of the four.

q: The reaction shown is followed by IR. Which change shows that the starting alkene has been completely converted to product?
c: A broad band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> appears, and the weak bands near 3020 and 1670 cm<sup>−1</sup> disappear
A strong band near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> appears, and the weak band near 3020 cm<sup>−1</sup> disappears completely
A broad band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> appears, while the weak bands near 3020 and 1670 cm<sup>−1</sup> remain
A sharp band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a weak band near 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup> appear
h: First decide what functional group hydroboration–oxidation makes; then decide which starting-material bands must vanish.
w: Hydroboration–oxidation converts the alkene into an alcohol (trans-2-methylcyclohexanol). The product shows a broad O–H band near 3350 cm−1. Completion means the alkene bands are gone: the vinylic =C–H stretch near 3020 cm−1 and the C=C stretch near 1670 cm−1. So the best evidence is a broad 3350 cm−1 band appearing while the 3020 and 1670 cm−1 bands disappear.
x: A 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> band would mean a ketone; hydroboration–oxidation gives an alcohol, not a carbonyl compound.
If the =C–H and C=C bands are still there, some alkene remains, so the reaction is not complete.
A sharp 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup> band belong to a terminal alkyne, which is neither reactant nor product.

q: 1-Hexyne is treated as shown. How does the IR spectrum change on going from the starting material to the isolated product?
c: The sharp 3300 and weak 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup> bands disappear; a strong band appears near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>
The sharp 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> band disappears; a strong band near 1730 and a pair near 2720 and 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup> appear
The 2120 cm<sup>−1</sup> band disappears; a broad O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> appears and stays
The sharp 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> band remains; a strong band appears near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup>
h: Mercury-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov, and the first-formed enol does not survive.
w: Hg2+-catalyzed hydration adds water Markovnikov to give an enol that tautomerizes to the methyl ketone, 2-hexanone. The terminal alkyne bands (strong, sharp ≡C–H at 3300 cm−1; weak C≡C at 2120 cm−1) vanish and a strong ketone C=O appears near 1715 cm−1. The answer is loss of 3300 and 2120 cm−1, gain of 1715 cm−1.
x: A 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup> C=O with 2720/2820 cm<sup>−1</sup> bands is an aldehyde, the anti-Markovnikov product of hydroboration–oxidation, not of HgSO<sub>4</sub> hydration.
The enol is only an intermediate; it tautomerizes to the ketone, so no lasting O–H band appears.
Both alkyne carbons react, so the terminal ≡C–H (3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>) is gone in the product.

q: A compound with formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O shows no IR absorption above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup> and none between 1600 and 1700 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its strongest band is at 1745 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which structure fits?
h: C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O has two degrees of unsaturation. If one is a C=O and there is no C=C, what is the other? Then think about where the C=O band falls.
w: DBE = (2·5 + 2 − 8)/2 = 2. The strong 1745 cm−1 band is a C=O, and with no =C–H above 3000 cm−1 and no C=C near 1650 cm−1 the second unsaturation must be a ring. Ring strain in a five-membered ring raises a ketone C=O from 1715 to about 1745 cm−1. The compound is cyclopentanone.
x: 3-Penten-2-one is conjugated, so its C=O is lowered to about 1675 cm<sup>−1</sup>; it would also show a C=C band near 1630 cm<sup>−1</sup> and =C–H above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
4-Pentenal would show the aldehyde C–H pair (2720, 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup>), a vinylic =C–H near 3080 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C=C near 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
3-Cyclopenten-1-ol has a broad O–H near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no C=O; its =C–H stretch also lies above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Which compound shows C–H stretching absorptions both just above and just below 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>, but no band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>?
h: sp<sup>3</sup> C–H absorbs below 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>, sp<sup>2</sup> C–H just above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and sp C–H near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
w: The compound needs both sp2 C–H (3000–3100 cm−1) and sp3 C–H (2850–3000 cm−1) and no sp C–H (3300 cm−1). Cyclohexene has two vinylic C–H bonds and eight allylic/ring CH2 hydrogens, so it fits.
x: Cyclohexane has only sp<sup>3</sup> C–H bonds, so all of its C–H stretches are below 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
1-Hexyne has a terminal ≡C–H, which gives a strong, sharp band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Benzene has only aromatic sp<sup>2</sup> C–H bonds, so it has no C–H stretch below 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Neat liquid 1-butanol shows a broad O–H band centered near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>. In a very dilute CCl<sub>4</sub> solution, the same compound shows a sharp O–H band near 3620 cm<sup>−1</sup>. What is the best explanation?
c: Hydrogen bonding in the neat liquid weakens the O–H bonds by varying amounts; in dilute solution the O–H is free
CCl<sub>4</sub> absorbs strongly near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup> and hides the O–H band, leaving only a weak overtone near 3620 cm<sup>−1</sup>
In the neat liquid some alcohol is ionized to alkoxide, and the O<sup>−</sup> absorbs at a lower wavenumber than a free O–H does
Dilution increases the O–H bond dipole of each isolated molecule, which raises the O–H stretching wavenumber
h: Which intermolecular interaction is present in the pure liquid but nearly absent when the molecules are far apart?
w: An O–H that donates a hydrogen bond is slightly weakened (smaller force constant), so it absorbs at lower wavenumber. In the neat liquid there is a range of hydrogen-bonded clusters, which smears the band out and centers it near 3350 cm−1. In very dilute CCl4 most molecules are isolated, so the free, non-hydrogen-bonded O–H gives a sharp band near 3620 cm−1.
x: CCl<sub>4</sub> has no C–H or O–H bonds and is nearly transparent above 1600 cm<sup>−1</sup>; that is why it is used as an IR solvent.
An alcohol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16) is not ionized to alkoxide to any detectable extent in the pure liquid, and an alkoxide has no O–H stretch at all.
Bond dipole affects band intensity, not position; the position depends on the force constant and the reduced mass.

q: Which IR feature best distinguishes 1-hexyne (I) from 3-hexyne (II)?
c: A strong, sharp band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> in I only
A strong C≡C band near 2200 cm<sup>−1</sup> in II only
A C=C band near 1650 cm<sup>−1</sup> in I only
A broad band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> in II only
h: A vibration must change the molecule's dipole moment to absorb IR light. Look at the symmetry of each alkyne.
w: 1-Hexyne has a terminal ≡C–H bond, which gives a strong, sharp band near 3300 cm−1 (plus a weak C≡C near 2120 cm−1). 3-Hexyne has no ≡C–H, and its C≡C is symmetrically substituted, so stretching it hardly changes the dipole and the band is absent. The answer is the sharp 3300 cm−1 band, present in I only.
x: The symmetric C≡C of 3-hexyne is IR-inactive (no dipole change); if anything, the weak C≡C band belongs to 1-hexyne.
Neither compound has a C=C double bond, so neither absorbs near 1650 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
A broad band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> signals a hydrogen-bonded O–H or N–H; 3-hexyne has neither.

q: Which compound's C=C stretching band in the 1600–1680 cm<sup>−1</sup> region is absent or nearly absent?
h: IR intensity depends on how much the dipole moment changes during the vibration.
w: A vibration absorbs IR light only if it changes the dipole moment. In (E)-3-hexene the C=C carries identical groups arranged symmetrically (a center of symmetry), so stretching the C=C produces no dipole change and the band is IR-inactive. Unsymmetrical or polarized C=C bonds give visible bands.
x: 1-Hexene is monosubstituted and unsymmetrical, so its C=C stretch (about 1640 cm<sup>−1</sup>) is a clear medium band.
In ethyl vinyl ether the oxygen donates electron density into the C=C, polarizing it strongly, so its C=C band (about 1620 cm<sup>−1</sup>) is strong.
In 2-cyclohexenone the C=C is conjugated with and polarized by the C=O, so it gives a medium-to-strong band near 1620 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NO gives the IR spectrum shown. There is no absorption between 3100 and 3600 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which structure fits?
h: The strong 1650 cm<sup>−1</sup> band suggests an amide. Then count the N–H bonds each candidate has.
w: A strong band at 1650 cm−1 is the low-frequency C=O of an amide (nitrogen lone-pair donation lowers the C=O bond order). The absence of any N–H stretch (3100–3600 cm−1) requires a tertiary amide with no N–H bond. The answer is N,N-dimethylacetamide.
x: Butanamide is a primary amide: its NH<sub>2</sub> gives two N–H bands near 3350 and 3180 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
N-Ethylacetamide is a secondary amide with one N–H, which gives a band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>.
Morpholine is a secondary amine and ether: it shows an N–H band near 3330 cm<sup>−1</sup> and has no C=O to absorb at 1650 cm<sup>−1</sup>.

q: Which compound gives the IR spectrum shown?
h: Besides the C=O band, look for a pair of medium bands just to the right of the ordinary C–H stretches.
w: The strong 1730 cm−1 band is a C=O, and the two medium bands at 2820 and 2720 cm−1 are the characteristic aldehyde C–H stretches (a Fermi-resonance doublet). Together they identify an aldehyde: hexanal.
x: 2-Hexanone is a ketone; its C=O is near 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and it has no aldehyde C–H, so no 2720/2820 cm<sup>−1</sup> pair.
Ethyl butanoate is an ester: C=O near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup> plus strong C–O bands near 1180 cm<sup>−1</sup>, but no 2720 cm<sup>−1</sup> aldehyde C–H band.
Hexanoic acid would show a very broad O–H spanning 2500–3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>, which this spectrum lacks.

q: Which pair of compounds would be hardest to tell apart using only the functional-group region (above 1500 cm<sup>−1</sup>) of their IR spectra?
h: IR identifies functional groups. Which pair has exactly the same functional group in nearly the same environment?
w: 2-Pentanone and 3-pentanone are both saturated acyclic ketones: each shows a strong C=O near 1715 cm−1 and only sp3 C–H stretches. Their differences are confined to the fingerprint region, which is why IR alone is a poor tool for telling such isomers apart (NMR does it easily).
x: Pentanal shows the aldehyde C–H pair at 2720 and 2820 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a C=O near 1730 cm<sup>−1</sup>; 2-pentanone has neither feature.
1-Pentanol has a strong, broad O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>; the ether has none, so they are easy to distinguish.
1-Pentyne has a strong, sharp ≡C–H band near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>; the internal alkyne 2-pentyne does not.

q: A C–H stretch appears at 2950 cm−1. Hooke's law gives ν̃ ∝ √(k/μ), where μ = m1m2/(m1 + m2). Assuming the force constant k is unchanged, at about what wavenumber should the corresponding C–D stretch appear? (Use masses 12, 1 and 2.)
h: Compute the reduced mass for C–H and for C–D, then scale the wavenumber by the square root of their ratio.
w: μ(C–H) = (12·1)/13 = 0.923; μ(C–D) = (12·2)/14 = 1.714. Since ν̃ ∝ 1/√μ, ν̃(C–D) = 2950 × √(0.923/1.714) = 2950 × 0.734 ≈ 2165 cm−1. This is why deuterated solvents and C–D labels show bands near 2100–2200 cm−1.
x: A heavier isotope must lower the wavenumber, not raise it; 4170 cm<sup>−1</sup> comes from multiplying by √2 instead of dividing.
1475 cm<sup>−1</sup> halves the wavenumber, as if ν̃ were proportional to 1/μ and μ doubled; the dependence is on the square root, and μ does not double.
2085 cm<sup>−1</sup> divides by √2, using the H/D mass ratio instead of the reduced masses; because carbon also moves, μ rises by less than a factor of 2.

q: The ≡C–H stretch of a terminal alkyne (about 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>) is higher than the =C–H stretch of an alkene (about 3080 cm<sup>−1</sup>) or the C–H stretch of an alkane (about 2900 cm<sup>−1</sup>). Why?
c: Greater s character in the sp carbon orbital makes the C–H bond shorter and stiffer
The ≡C–H hydrogen forms hydrogen bonds, which raise its stretching wavenumber
The sp carbon is lighter than an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon, which lowers the reduced mass
The ≡C–H bond is the weakest of the three, so it vibrates fastest
h: All three bonds join the same two atoms, so the reduced mass is the same. What about the force constant?
w: Wavenumber depends on the force constant and the reduced mass. The masses are identical (C and H), so the difference comes from k. An sp orbital has 50% s character (sp2 33%, sp3 25%), so the ≡C–H bond is shorter and stronger, with a larger force constant. The answer is greater s character gives a stiffer bond.
x: Hydrogen bonding weakens the X–H bond and lowers its stretching wavenumber, and alkyne C–H is only a very weak hydrogen-bond donor anyway.
Hybridization does not change an atom's mass; the reduced mass of every C–H bond is the same.
The ≡C–H bond is the strongest of the three, and a weaker bond (smaller k) vibrates at lower, not higher, wavenumber.
